---
title: "Log-Based Recovery"
---

## How Data Moves: The Access Model

Data lives on **disk** (physical blocks) and is loaded into **memory** (buffer blocks) when needed.

- `input(B)` — load block B from disk into memory buffer.
- `output(B)` — flush buffer block B back to disk.

Inside a transaction:

- `read(X)` — copy data item X from buffer into the transaction's local variable.
- `write(X)` — copy the local variable back into the buffer block.

---

## Log-Based Recovery

The key idea: before touching the database, every change is first recorded in a **log** on stable storage. If a crash happens, the log tells us exactly what to undo or redo. A log is kept on stable storage. The log is a sequence of log records, which maintains information about update activities on the database.

**Log record types:**

| Record | Written when |
|---|---|
| `< Ti start >` | Transaction begins |
| `< Ti, X, V1, V2 >` | Before writing X — V1 is the old value, V2 is the new value |
| `< Ti commit >` | Transaction completes successfully |
| `< Ti abort >` | Transaction is rolled back |

A transaction is considered **committed** the moment its commit log record reaches stable storage — even if the actual data changes are still sitting in the buffer.

---

## Database Modification Schemes

| Scheme | When updates hit disk |
|---|---|
| **Immediate modification** | Anytime — before or after commit |
| **Deferred modification** | Only at commit time |

We focus on **immediate modification** — it requires both undo and redo during recovery, but it is the more commonly used approach.

#### Example
 
![](immediate_modification_scheme_example.png)

| Scenario | Log state at crash | Recovery action |
|---|---|---|
| **(a)** | T0 started but neither committed nor aborted | **Undo T0** — restore B to 2000, then A to 1000 |
| **(b)** | T0 committed; T1 started but not committed | **Redo T0** (set A=950, B=2050); **Undo T1** (restore C to 700) |
| **(c)** | Both T0 and T1 committed | **Redo T0** then **Redo T1** (set A=950, B=2050, C=600) |

---

## Undo and Redo

When a crash happens, the recovery system needs to either reverse incomplete work or replay committed work that didn't make it to disk.

| Operation | What it does | Direction | When used |
|---|---|---|---|
| `undo(Ti)` | Restores all writes to old values (V1) | Scans log **backwards** | Ti started but never committed |
| `redo(Ti)` | Reapplies all writes to new values (V2) | Scans log **forwards** | Ti committed but data may not be on disk |

During undo, each restored value is recorded as a **Compensation Log Record (CLR)**: `< Ti, X, V1 >`. When the undo is complete, `< Ti abort >` is written.

---

## Deciding What to Do After a Crash

| Log contains | Action |
|---|---|
| `< Ti start >` but no commit or abort | **Undo** Ti |
| `< Ti start >` and `< Ti commit >` or `< Ti abort >` | **Redo** Ti |

---

## Checkpoints

Without checkpoints, recovery would replay the entire log from the very beginning — extremely slow for a database that has been running for a long time. A **checkpoint** flushes all buffered writes to disk and records which transactions are currently active. Recovery only needs to look at the log from the checkpoint onwards.

**Steps during checkpointing:**

1. Output all in-memory log records to stable storage.
2. Flush all modified buffer blocks to disk.
3. Write a `< checkpoint L >` record, where L is the list of active transactions.

**After a crash, for each transaction relative to the last checkpoint:**

| Transaction state | Action |
|---|---|
| Committed **before** checkpoint | Ignore — already safely on disk |
| Committed **after** checkpoint | Redo |
| Still active at time of crash | Undo |
